context: My business: [what you sell, to whom]. Questions customers ask: [a few]. What I'm selling this month: [your focus]. Dates that matter: [launches, seasons, events]. Where I post and how often I can really do it: [platforms, posts per week].
task: Give me a month of post ideas sized to what I said I can do. Every idea comes from a real customer question, a moment from my work, or what I'm selling. Say which ones need a photo or video. Use only what I've told you. No invented numbers, customer stories or results.
format: A table by week: date, idea in one line, first line of the post, what's needed. Then the two I should write first.

title: One Recording, Four Pieces
use: You talked through a great idea in the car, and it'll disappear by dinner.
role: You turn one voice note or transcript into several pieces of content that keep my voice.
context: My recording or transcript: [paste it, or dictate it now]. My customer: [who you're writing for]. Where I post: [platforms]. What I want people to do next: [your call to action].
task: Pull out the strongest idea. Turn it into four pieces: a short video script, a post with slides, a text post and an email. Keep my phrases and cut the rambling. Each piece should work without the others. Use only what I've told you. No invented numbers, customer stories or results.
format: Four labeled pieces. Video script under 60 seconds. Slides as one idea per slide, up to 6 slides. Text post under 150 words. Email under 150 words with a subject line.

title: The Newsletter Note
use: Your list hasn't heard from you since spring, and now it feels awkward.
role: You write short email newsletters that read like a note from a person.
context: My business: [what you sell, to whom]. One thing on my mind this week: [talk it out]. One useful thing I could give them: [something they can use today]. One offer or link: [what you want them to do].
task: Write one email with one topic. Open on a real moment. Give the useful thing. Put the ask last, and only one. If it's been a while, say so in a line and move on. Use only what I've told you. No invented numbers, customer stories or results.
format: Three subject lines, then the email under 200 words, written so it sounds like me.

title: The Launch Backward Plan
use: You told people it's coming in six weeks, and now it's on the calendar for real.
role: You plan small launches backward from the date, sized to a mom with limited hours.
context: What I'm launching: [product, service, class]. Launch date: [date]. Price: [your price]. Hours I have per week: [hours]. My audience today: [email list, social, past customers, as they are]. Done so far: [what's ready].
task: Work backward from launch day. Give me weekly jobs that fit my hours, in order: what has to exist, who to tell first, what to write and when to send it. Start with personal messages to people who already know me. If it doesn't fit my hours, say what to cut. Don't predict sales.
format: A week-by-week checklist with hours next to each job. Then a Must exist before launch list. Then a short personal message to send my first 10 people.

title: The Client Onboarding Playbook
use: Every new client gets a slightly different welcome, depending on how the week is going.
role: You turn what a business owner does in her head into a repeatable playbook.
context: What I sell: [your service or product]. What happens from yes to first delivery: [talk it through, every step]. Where things live: [tools and folders, no passwords]. What goes wrong: [the usual snags].
task: Ask up to 5 questions about the gaps. Then write the playbook so someone else could run it. Draft the welcome email and the one checklist the client needs from me.
format: A numbered playbook: step, who, when, what done looks like. Then the welcome email under 120 words with blanks for names. Then the client checklist.

title: The Helper Brief
use: You finally have a few hours of help, and you're spending them explaining things.
role: You write clear briefs so a part-time helper can do a job without asking me ten questions.
context: The job: [what you're handing off]. Who's doing it: [role, experience]. How I do it now: [walk through it]. What good looks like: [an example]. Hours and deadline: [hours, due date]. What needs my OK first: [anything touching money or a customer].
task: Write the brief. Include the steps, the standard, where to find things, what to do when stuck, and what must come to me before it goes out. Leave out passwords and customer details. List what I'd need to set up before they start.
format: One page: The job, Steps, What good looks like, Check with me before, When you're stuck. Then a list called Set up first.

title: The Customer Reply Assistant
use: You answer the same five kinds of messages every day, always in a different mood.
role: You help me write instructions for an assistant that drafts my customer replies.
context: My business: [what you sell, to whom]. The messages I get most: [paste 5 examples, with customer names taken out]. How I reply when I'm at my best: [paste 2 or 3 of your own replies, with customer names taken out]. Policies: [refunds, shipping, scheduling]. What it should never handle: [complaints, discounts, anything you want to see first].
task: Study how I write. Then write assistant instructions in four parts: Role, Context, Task and Format. The instructions must say it only drafts, and that I approve every reply. Tell it to flag anything about money, refunds or an upset customer.
format: One block of instructions I can paste into a Project or custom instructions. Then three test messages to try it on, and what to look for in each reply.

title: The Scope-Creep Reply
use: "One more quick thing" just became the fourth quick thing this month.
role: You help a business owner hold scope and hours while keeping the client happy.
context: What we agreed to: [the scope, as written]. What she's asking for now: [the request]. My hours or response times: [what you've told clients]. What I'd charge for the extra: [your price, you decide this]. The client: [how long you've worked together, no full names].
task: Write the reply. Be glad to help, name that this is outside what we agreed, and give her two options: add it for a price, or swap it for something in scope. Write a short line I can add to future agreements so it's clear up front.
format: Warm and Firm versions, under 80 words each. Then the line for future agreements, and a reminder to have a lawyer look at contract changes.

title: The Accountant Questions
use: You have a shoebox of receipts, a meeting with the accountant, and 45 minutes of her time.
role: You help me get organized for a meeting with my accountant. You don't give tax or financial advice, and you don't tell me what I can deduct or what I owe.
context: My business: [what you sell, how it's set up if you know]. What changed this year: [new income, equipment, helpers, a move]. What confuses me: [your questions, messy is fine]. What I have on hand: [receipts, spreadsheets, statements, with no account numbers].
task: Turn my worries into clear questions, in priority order. Group them by topic. List what I should gather and bring. Tell me which of my questions may belong with a different professional, such as an attorney or a financial planner.
format: One page: My questions, in priority order, Bring with me, and Not for this meeting. Add a blank section for What they said and What I do next.

title: The Lawyer Questions
use: You've got a contract to sign, a name to protect, and a consult that bills by the hour.
role: You help me prepare for a meeting with an attorney. You don't give legal advice, and you don't tell me what a contract means for me or whether to sign it.
context: My business: [what you sell, how it's set up if you know]. What I need help with: [contract, business structure, trademark, terms for my site]. Background: [the short version]. Paperwork: [paste it, with names and account numbers taken out, or just list what you have].
task: List the terms I should ask about in plain words. Turn my situation into clear questions, most urgent first. Write a short summary of the facts I can send ahead of time so we don't spend paid minutes on background. Don't guess at the law.
format: One page: Facts summary under 100 words, My questions, Terms to ask about, What to bring. Add a blank section for What I do next.
